learn.title: can / can't: ability
learn.html:
We use it to say what you know or can do. In Spanish we use two different verbs; in English, for ability, we always use can.

Form: subject + can / can't + verb in base form. Can is the same for all persons: no -s and no to. The full form cannot also exists.

AffirmativeNegativeQuestionShort answer
She can swim.She can't swim.Can she swim?Yes, she can. / No, she can't.
I can sing.I can't sing.Can you sing?Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
They can speak Italian.They can't speak Italian.Can they speak Italian?Yes, they can. / No, they can't.
  • The short affirmative answer uses can alone, with no verb: Yes, he can.
  • To contrast two abilities: I can't read music, but I can play the piano.
  • With good at we use verb + -ing: She is good at singing.

watch.why: After can, use the base form, without -s.

watch.wrong: They can to play the guitar.

watch.why: Can makes the question on its own, without do/does.

words.es: cocinar (traditional dishes, Chinese food, dinner, Russian food)
tocar un instrumento / jugar (the piano, the guitar, chess, a sport)
manejar (a car, to work, to school)

learn.title: Adverbs of manner
learn.html:
They tell how someone does an action. Most end in -ly, such as quickly. Form: adjective + -ly.

RuleAdjective → Adverb
Regular: + -lyslow → slowly, quick → quickly, careful → carefully, quiet → quietly, fluent → fluently
Ends in -y: y → i + -lyeasy → easily, noisy → noisily, happy → happily, angry → angrily
Ends in -le: drop the ecomfortable → comfortably
Ends in -ful: + -lybeautiful → beautifully
Irregulargood → well, fast → fast

Position: after the verb or after the object: She can't dance well. He speaks Chinese fluently. With can't: Sam can't swim fast.

Good describes nouns (a good singer); well describes actions (sings well).

watch.wrong: She can very well play the piano.
watch.right: She can play the piano very well.
watch.why: The adverb goes at the end, not between the verb and its object.
With a verb we use the adverb well, not the adjective good.

watch.wrong: I cook very well Italian food.
watch.right: I cook Italian food very well.
watch.why: The adverb goes after the object.
There is no fastly: fast is both an adjective and an adverb.

learn.title: Strategy: showing interest
learn.html:
When someone tells you about a talent, react to show interest. Intonation matters: if your voice goes up, you sound interested; if it is almost flat, you sound cold.

  • Wow, that's amazing! / That's incredible! — strong admiration.
  • Really? I love Thai food. — interest and something about yourself.
  • Yeah? / Really? — ask the person to keep talking (voice goes up).
  • Ah, that's nice. / That's good. — a colder answer: shows little interest.

I do crosswords on the bus.

learn.title: like / love + verb with -ing
learn.html:
We use it to talk about activities you like. After like, love and good at, the verb takes -ing. In Spanish, we use the infinitive instead.

StructureExample
like / love + verb-ingDominic likes visiting archaeological sites. Brianna loves making new things.
be (not) good at + verb-ingI'm good at reading fast. I'm not good at playing basketball.
go + activity-ing (no to)Dean likes going snowboarding.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• Wow, that's amazing! / That's incredible! — show admiration.
  • Really? I love Thai food. — show interest and add something about yourself.
  • Can you …? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't. — ask about abilities.
  • I'm good at … / I'm not good at … + -ing — talk about your strengths and weaknesses.
  • I'm … because … — give a reason: I'm optimistic because I never feel sad.
  • Be honest. / Be patient. — give short advice.
  • He's not very patient. — soften a criticism.

reading.title: Talent Night at Casa Verde
reading.intro: Read the talent show ad and answer.
paragraphs: Do you have a talent? Come to Talent Night at the Casa Verde Community Center on Saturday, March 15, at 7:00 p.m. Everybody can take part. You can sing, dance, tell jokes or play an instrument. You don't need to be a professional. You only need to be brave and friendly!

Last year there were ten contestants. Marta, a patient teacher, sang an old song beautifully. Tomás, a quiet student, played the guitar very well. Rafa, a comedian, was very funny. He can't sing and he can't dance, but he tells jokes really well, and the audience laughed a lot.

This year there are three prizes: $200, $100 and $50. The judges are a music teacher, a chef and a dancer. They like talented people, but they also like contestants who are honest and relaxed. Tickets cost $5. To join, send an email before March 10. Each person has only four minutes, so practice slowly and carefully at home. Good luck!

Yes, I can. I can play the piano and the guitar, but I can't play the violin.
Wow, that's amazing! Can you sing too?
Yes, I can, but not very well. I'm good at dancing. I take salsa classes on Tuesdays.
Yes! I cook Mexican food very well. I can also speak French, but I speak it slowly.
Incredible! And what can't you do?
I can't drive a car. My brother drives, and he drives very fast!
